opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the appeal of the private language argument, at least as I read it, is that it goes right to the heart of what makes dualism seem so compelling in the first place. The dualist intuition is something like this: I have my inner experiences, the redness of red, the painfulness of pain, and these are things that only I have direct access to. Everything outside, all the behaviour and the brain activity, is just the public shadow of this private realm. And that picture leads you very naturally to the so-called hard problem, because now there seems to be this unbridgeable gap between the private, subjective world and the public, objective one.

What Wittgenstein does is ask: suppose you really did have a purely private sensation, and you wanted to name it. He gives the example of keeping a diary, writing "S" every time a certain sensation occurs. But what would make it correct or incorrect to write "S" on a later occasion? There's no criterion of correctness available, because the only check is my own impression that this is the same sensation as before. And as he puts it, whatever seems right to me is right, which just means we can't talk about "right" at all. So the idea of a word whose meaning is fixed by a purely private object begins to dissolve.

Now, it's important to be careful here. Wittgenstein isn't denying that we have sensations. He's not a behaviourist in the crude sense. He says the sensation is "not a something, but not a nothing either." The point is that our words for experience get their meaning from a shared form of life, from public practices, expressions of pain, the way we respond to each other. The grammar of experience talk is rooted in that public world.

And that's why I find it such a powerful challenge. Once you see that, the metaphysical picture of a hidden inner realm, with a gulf separating it from the physical, starts to look like a philosophical illusion produced by misunderstanding how our language works. The hard problem isn't solved so much as it's loosened. You stop feeling the pull of the question in quite the same way.

This matters a great deal for thinking about AI, actually. If consciousness were a purely private, metaphysically hidden property, then the question "Is this large language model conscious?" would have a fact of the matter that might be forever inaccessible to us. But if our concept of consciousness is grounded in shared practices, in how we encounter and engage with other beings, then the question becomes partly about whether these new kinds of entities can be brought into that form of life, and how our language might have to stretch to accommodate them. That's a much more productive way to approach it, I think, than worrying about some ineffable inner light that's either on or off.

r001.rationale: It describes a purely private sensation as something only the speaker has direct access to and discusses assigning it the private label “S.”

r002.rationale: It says there is no criterion of correctness for reapplying “S” beyond the speaker’s own impression, so the word’s meaning begins to dissolve.

r003.rationale: The response says a sensation is “not a something, but not a nothing either,” but does not communicate that nothing would serve as well as an unsayable something.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the private language argument gets at something that's very hard to see when you're in the grip of the Cartesian picture. The Cartesian picture is that each of us has this inner theatre, this private realm of experience that only I have access to, and the words I use for my sensations, words like "pain," get their meaning by being attached to those private inner objects. I look inward, I find the pain, I label it. And then the dualist asks, well, how could any amount of physical description, any amount of talk about neurons, ever capture that inner thing? And that's the explanatory gap, that's the hard problem, and so on.

What Wittgenstein does is he asks you to take that picture really seriously and then see whether it can actually be made to work. Suppose I try to set up a language in which a sign "S" refers to a particular sensation, and I define it purely privately, by inward ostension, by concentrating my attention on the sensation and saying "this is S." Then the next day I have a sensation and I say, "ah, that's S again." The question is, what's the difference between my correctly applying the word and merely seeming to myself to apply it correctly? There's nothing to check against. There's no criterion of correctness independent of my own impression. And as he puts it, whatever is going to seem right to me is right, and that only means we can't talk about right here at all. So the word has no use. It isn't doing anything.

And the crucial move for me is the beetle in the box. Everybody has a box, nobody can look in anyone else's box, and everyone says there's a beetle in theirs. Wittgenstein's point is that the thing in the box plays no role in the language game. It could be anything, it could be constantly changing, the box could even be empty, and the word "beetle" would still function exactly as it does. So the private object, considered as a private object, drops out of consideration as irrelevant. Our concept of pain, our concept of experience, is woven into public life, into behaviour, into how we respond to each other, into the practices of comforting and treating and so on. That's where the meaning lives.

Now, the reason I think that's a powerful challenge to dualism is that dualism depends entirely on the intelligibility of the private object. The dualist needs there to be this thing, the quale, the raw feel, that's conceptually separable from everything public, so that you can imagine it absent, as with zombies, or inverted, as with the spectrum. Wittgenstein's argument suggests that when you try to think about that thing in isolation from its place in our lives, you're not actually thinking about anything determinate. You've got a picture, and the picture is very compelling, but it's doing no work.

I should say, and this is important, this isn't behaviourism, and it isn't denying that we have experiences. Wittgenstein says explicitly that it's not a nothing, but it's not a something either. The point isn't to eliminate the inner. It's to resist the move of reifying the inner into a mysterious kind of object that then generates the metaphysical problem. And I find that enormously liberating, because once you make that move, questions about consciousness, including the questions we now have about large language models and whether there's anything it's like to be them, become questions about forms of life and patterns of behaviour and how we're able to make sense of a thing, rather than questions about the presence or absence of some occult inner ingredient that we could never in principle detect anyway.

r001.rationale: The response describes a sensation sign defined privately by inward attention and emphasizes that only the speaker has access to the inner experience.

r002.rationale: It says there is no criterion independent of the speaker’s impression for checking whether the private sensation word is correctly applied, so the word has no use.

r003.rationale: The response explains that the beetle could be anything or the box could be empty while “beetle” functions the same, conveying that an inaccessible private something is no more useful than nothing.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think its power comes from questioning the picture that makes dualism seem so natural in the first place. We imagine an inner world of private objects—my pains, my experiences of red—which I can inspect directly, while you can only infer their existence from my behaviour. And then we ask how that private world relates to the physical world.

Wittgenstein asks us to look at how words like “pain” actually acquire their meaning. Suppose I try to name a sensation privately, and then use that name whenever the same sensation recurs. What distinguishes using the name correctly from merely thinking that I’m using it correctly? If there’s no independent criterion, then that distinction seems to disappear. And that undermines the idea that our language of experience gets its meaning simply by attaching labels to objects in an inaccessible inner realm.

The beetle-in-the-box analogy makes this very vivid. Everyone has a box, everyone calls what’s inside their box a beetle, but nobody can look inside anyone else’s. Whatever is in the box cannot play the role we imagined in establishing the public meaning of “beetle.”

Now, that isn’t a denial that we have experiences. If I’m in pain, Wittgenstein isn’t telling me that nothing is happening! Nor is it a straightforward proof of physicalism. It’s a challenge to a particular conception of experience, one that generates the dualist problem. Our talk about consciousness belongs within our shared human life. Once you take that seriously, the idea of consciousness as an intrinsically private thing, whose connection to everything else is forever mysterious, begins to lose its grip.

r001.rationale: The response describes privately naming a sensation that the speaker can inspect while others cannot access it directly.

r002.rationale: It asks what distinguishes correct use of a private sensation-word from merely thinking it is correct, and says there is no independent criterion.

r003.rationale: The beetle analogy says the box’s contents cannot establish public meaning, but the response does not state that nothing would serve as well as an unsayable something.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think its power lies in challenging the picture that makes dualism seem so natural in the first place. We imagine that there’s this private inner realm, populated by experiences that only I can inspect, and that words like “pain” acquire their meaning by referring to things in that realm.

Wittgenstein asks us to examine how that could work. Suppose I privately name a sensation and then try to use that name whenever the same sensation recurs. What distinguishes using it correctly from merely thinking I’m using it correctly? If whatever seems right to me counts as right, then we’ve lost the distinction between following a rule and believing that we’re following one.

The point isn’t that pain doesn’t exist, or that other people have to verify every experience I report. It’s that our language about experience gets its meaning within a shared human life: how we learn these words, the circumstances in which we use them, how we respond to one another. It doesn’t get its meaning through private acts of pointing at inner objects.

So I wouldn’t say this is a knockdown proof against every possible form of dualism. But it undermines a very compelling motivation for it. Once you stop treating consciousness as a collection of private objects, the question of how those objects connect to the physical world starts to look rather different.

r001.rationale: It describes the imagined private inner realm as containing experiences only the speaker can inspect, with words like “pain” referring to things in that realm.

r002.rationale: It asks what could distinguish correct use of a private sensation-word from merely thinking it is correct, and says that if whatever seems right counts, the distinction between following a rule and believing one is following it disappears.

r003.rationale: The response does not communicate Wittgenstein’s claim that nothing would serve as well as a something about which nothing can be said.
